nmr-ms-001.question: Which substance is generally used as the δ = 0 ppm reference for ¹H NMR chemical shifts?
nmr-ms-001.explanation: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) has 12 equivalent protons that give a single sharp singlet. Silicon is less electronegative than carbon, so the TMS protons are strongly shielded and appear upfield (to the right) of the signals of almost all organic compounds. This is defined as δ = 0 ppm, and chemical shifts are expressed in ppm, the offset from the reference (Hz) divided by the spectrometer frequency (MHz). CDCl3 and D2O are deuterated solvents for measurement and are also used to stabilize the field (the lock). The small amount of residual protonated solvent (such as CHCl3 at δ 7.26) is sometimes used as a secondary reference, but the 0 ppm reference is TMS.

nmr-ms-002.question: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of propanal, CH3CH2CHO, which chemical shift is closest to where the aldehyde proton (−CHO) signal appears?
nmr-ms-002.explanation: The aldehyde proton is strongly deshielded both because the bond to the highly electronegative oxygen pulls electrons away and because of the magnetic anisotropy created by the π electrons of C=O, so it appears very far downfield, at δ 9–10. It rarely overlaps with other signals, which makes it convenient for confirming an aldehyde. δ about 2.4 is typical of the CH2 next to the carbonyl (the α position) and δ about 1.1 of the terminal CH3; both are in propanal, but neither is the aldehyde proton. The COOH proton of a carboxylic acid appears even further downfield, as a broad signal around δ 10–13.

nmr-ms-003.question: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of bromoethane, CH3CH2Br, what splitting pattern does the CH2 signal show?
nmr-ms-003.explanation: Splitting by spin–spin coupling is set by the number n of equivalent protons on the neighboring carbon, and the signal splits into n + 1 lines (the n + 1 rule). The CH2 has the three protons of CH3 next to it, so it becomes a quartet of 3 + 1 = 4 lines, with intensities of 1:3:3:1 following Pascal's triangle. Conversely, the CH3 signal becomes a triplet (1:2:1) from the two protons of the neighboring CH2. A triplet mistakes this for the CH3 signal. A singlet overlooks the splitting by the neighboring CH3 (equivalent protons on the same carbon do not split each other, and neither does bromine). The CH2 is deshielded by bromine's electron withdrawal and appears at δ about 3.4.

nmr-ms-004.question: Which pair gives the number of signals and the integration ratio in the ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-chloropropane, (CH3)2CHCl?
nmr-ms-004.explanation: The two methyl groups are interchanged by the molecule's mirror plane, so the six protons are chemically equivalent and give one signal. The central CH proton is a single proton with its own signal. There are therefore two signals with an integration ratio of 6:1. The methyl groups become a doublet (δ about 1.5) from the neighboring CH, and the CH becomes a septet (δ about 4.1) from the six neighboring protons. 3:1 counts the two equivalent methyl groups as only one, and 3:3:1 treats the two methyl groups as separate signals. The integration ratio represents the ratio of the numbers of protons.

nmr-ms-005.question: Of CH3F, CH3Cl and CH3I, which has its methyl protons furthest downfield (largest δ)?
nmr-ms-005.explanation: When a highly electronegative atom is attached, electrons around the proton are pulled away and shielding weakens (deshielding), so the signal moves downfield (to larger δ). The electronegativities of the halogens run F (4.0) > Cl (3.2) > I (2.7), and the methyl chemical shifts are about 4.3 ppm for CH3F, about 3.1 ppm for CH3Cl and about 2.2 ppm for CH3I. Thinking that the large, heavy iodine comes furthest downfield is wrong; here electronegativity is what mainly determines the chemical shift. Note that the CH3F signal is a doublet because of spin–spin coupling with ¹⁹F (spin 1/2).

nmr-ms-006.question: How many signals appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum (fully proton-decoupled) of 1,4-dimethylbenzene (p-xylene), CH3−C6H4−CH3?
nmr-ms-006.explanation: p-Xylene is highly symmetric: the two methyl carbons are equivalent and give one signal, the ring carbons bearing the methyl groups (C1 and C4) are also equivalent and give one, and the remaining four CH ring carbons (C2, C3, C5, C6) are all equivalent and give one, for a total of three. Eight counts every carbon in the molecule separately, and four is the number of signals for o-xylene (1,2-dimethylbenzene). In m-xylene there are four kinds of ring carbon, which with the methyl carbon gives five. The number of ¹³C NMR signals is thus useful for telling isomers apart by their symmetry.

nmr-ms-007.question: On a 400 MHz NMR spectrometer, a proton signal appears 2920 Hz downfield of TMS. What is the chemical shift of this signal?
nmr-ms-007.explanation: The chemical shift is δ = offset from the reference (Hz) / spectrometer frequency (MHz), so 2920 / 400 = 7.30 ppm. δ around 7.3 is the typical region for aromatic protons. Expressed in ppm, the value is independent of the spectrometer frequency: the same proton measured on a 600 MHz instrument has an offset that grows to 7.30 × 600 = 4380 Hz, but δ remains 7.30. The coupling constant J, by contrast, is expressed in Hz and does not change between instruments. δ 2.92 divides the Hz value by 1000, and δ 73.0 is off by an order of magnitude, far outside the usual ¹H NMR range (roughly 0–13 ppm).

nmr-ms-008.question: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of a mixture of ethanol, CH3CH2OH, and acetone, CH3COCH3, the integration ratio of the ethanol CH3 triplet to the acetone singlet is 1.0 : 4.0. What is the molar ratio of ethanol to acetone in the mixture?
nmr-ms-008.explanation: Integrals are proportional to the number of protons contributing to the signal. The ethanol CH3 has 3H per molecule, and acetone has 6H per molecule from its two equivalent methyl groups, so per proton the values are 1.0/3 = 0.33 for ethanol and 4.0/6 = 0.67 for acetone, giving a molar ratio of 1 : 2. 1 : 4 takes the integration ratio directly as the molar ratio, and 2 : 1 reverses the ratio. Comparing integrals divided by proton counts in this way gives the molar ratio of components without reference standards, and adding an internal standard of known purity also gives the content (quantitative NMR, qNMR).

nmr-ms-009.question: In the mass spectrum of an organic compound, peaks at m/z 122 and m/z 124 appear with nearly 1 : 1 intensity in the molecular-ion region. Which element is the compound thought to contain?
nmr-ms-009.explanation: Bromine has two isotopes, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, in a ratio of nearly 1 : 1 (about 50.7% and 49.3%), so a molecule containing one bromine shows M and M+2 peaks, two mass units apart, of nearly equal intensity. 1-Bromopropane, C3H7Br, for example, gives m/z 122 and 124. For chlorine, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl are roughly 3 : 1, so M : M+2 ≈ 3 : 1. The nitrogen isotope ¹⁵N is only about 0.4%, and no large M+2 peak results. With two bromines, M : M+2 : M+4 ≈ 1 : 2 : 1.

nmr-ms-010.question: Which correctly describes the molecular-ion region of the mass spectrum of chlorobenzene, C6H5Cl? Take mass numbers as C = 12, H = 1, ³⁵Cl = 35 and ³⁷Cl = 37.
choices: Peaks at m/z 112 and m/z 114 appear with an intensity ratio of about 3 : 1
Peaks at m/z 112 and m/z 114 appear with an intensity ratio of about 1 : 1
Peaks at m/z 112 and m/z 113 appear with an intensity ratio of about 3 : 1
nmr-ms-010.explanation: The mass of C6H5³⁵Cl is 6×12 + 5×1 + 35 = 112, and that of C6H5³⁷Cl is 114. Natural chlorine is about 75.8% ³⁵Cl and about 24.2% ³⁷Cl, so the intensity ratio M (112) : M+2 (114) is about 3 : 1. About 1 : 1 is the case for bromine (⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br) and confuses it with chlorine. m/z 113 is the M+1 peak containing one ¹³C, only a small peak of about 6.6% of M (1.1% × 6) for a six-carbon molecule. The chlorine isotopes differ in mass by 2, so the isotope peak appears at M+2, not M+1.

nmr-ms-011.question: An organic compound containing only C, H, N and O shows its molecular-ion peak at m/z 73. What can be said about the number of nitrogen atoms in this compound?
choices: Nothing can be said from the molecular-ion mass alone
nmr-ms-011.explanation: By the nitrogen rule, for molecules made of C, H, N and O (and halogens, S and so on), an odd number of nitrogen atoms gives an odd molecular weight (nominal mass), and zero or an even number gives an even one. This is because, among the common elements, only nitrogen has an even mass number (14) and an odd valence (3). m/z 73 is odd, so the number of nitrogens is odd; diethylamine, C4H11N (4×12 + 11 + 14 = 73), for example, fits. An even molecular weight means zero or an even number of nitrogens. Note that the rule holds for molecular ions and does not apply directly to fragment ions.

nmr-ms-012.question: In the electron-ionization mass spectrum of neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane), C(CH3)4 (molecular weight 72), at what m/z does the most intense peak (the base peak) appear?
nmr-ms-012.explanation: The molecular ion of neopentane, C(CH3)4⁺· (m/z 72), immediately becomes the stable tert-butyl cation, (CH3)3C⁺ (72 − 15 = 57), when one methyl group leaves the central quaternary carbon. This cleavage happens so readily that m/z 57 is the base peak and the molecular-ion peak is barely observed. m/z 15 is the methyl cation, CH3⁺, but the methyl cation is very unstable and does not give a strong peak. That the positive charge tends to stay on the more stable carbocation fragment is the basic principle for interpreting fragments. For compounds whose molecular ion is hard to see, confirm the molecular weight with a soft ionization method such as chemical ionization.

nmr-ms-013.question: In the electron-ionization mass spectrum of 2-hexanone, CH3COCH2CH2CH2CH3 (molecular weight 100), at what m/z does the ion formed by the McLafferty rearrangement appear?
nmr-ms-013.explanation: The McLafferty rearrangement occurs in compounds with a hydrogen on the carbon γ to the carbonyl group. Through a six-membered transition state, the γ-hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen, the bond between the α and β carbons breaks, and a neutral alkene is lost. In 2-hexanone the γ carbon is C5, so propene, CH2=CHCH3 (mass 42), is lost, giving the enol radical cation CH2=C(OH)CH3⁺· (100 − 42 = 58). m/z 43 is the acetylium ion CH3CO⁺ from α-cleavage next to the carbonyl, and m/z 85 is C4H9CO⁺ from α-cleavage with loss of a methyl radical; neither involves a rearrangement.

nmr-ms-014.question: In high-resolution mass spectrometry, an ion's m/z is measured as 28.0313. Which ion is most appropriate? Take the exact masses as ¹H = 1.00783, ¹²C = 12.00000, ¹⁴N = 14.00307 and ¹⁶O = 15.99491, and ignore the electron mass.
nmr-ms-014.explanation: All three have a nominal mass of 28, but their exact masses differ. CO is 12.00000 + 15.99491 = 27.9949, N2 is 2 × 14.00307 = 28.0061, and C2H4 is 2 × 12.00000 + 4 × 1.00783 = 28.0313, so C2H4⁺ matches the measurement. CO and N2 differ by about 0.011, and N2 and C2H4 by about 0.025, so separating them needs a resolving power m/Δm of a few thousand. Each hydrogen is about 0.008 heavier than its nominal mass and ¹⁶O is about 0.005 lighter, so the more H an ion contains, the more its exact mass exceeds the integer. High-resolution MS uses these differences to narrow down the molecular formula.

nmr-ms-015.question: A compound with molecular formula C3H6O shows a strong IR absorption at about 1715 cm⁻¹ and only a single singlet at δ 2.1 in its ¹H NMR spectrum. What is the compound?
nmr-ms-015.explanation: A strong absorption at about 1715 cm⁻¹ indicates C=O, and a ¹H NMR spectrum with only one singlet indicates that all the protons are equivalent and that there are no protons on neighboring carbons. In acetone, the two methyl groups (6H) are equivalent and are separated by the carbonyl carbon, so they do not split each other and give a single singlet at δ about 2.1. Propanal also has C=O (about 1725 cm⁻¹), but it shows three kinds of signal, including the aldehyde proton at δ about 9.8. 2-Propen-1-ol has no C=O and shows a broad O−H absorption (3200–3550 cm⁻¹) and several signals, including those of the alkene protons.
